newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Israel keeps far-flung Gaza families apart.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Israel keeps far-flung Gaza families apart.

text.p: Dalal Mousa's eyes welled up with tears when she learned her younger brother Abdel-Jawwad was not going to return home to Gaza for a visit this year.
Palestinian officials had just informed her that Israel had refused to give her five nephews permits to enter Gaza with their father, prompting the whole family to cancel plans for a homecoming.
"I have not seen my brother for 30 years. Don't they have any mercy," said the 62-year-old woman.
Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians live and work abroad, mostly in oil-rich Gulf Arab states, returning home once a year to spend the summer with relatives.
Apart from the joy of being united with their families, summer visits are regarded as a main source of income to the ailing economy in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
But Dalal, like thousands of other Gazans, may have to forego the long-awaited annual family reunion due to tighter Israeli restrictions on the entry of Palestinians.
ONLY A FRACTION ARRIVED THIS YEAR

Palestinian officials say the new restrictions on family visits, combined with an ongoing Israeli closure that makes travel in and out of the Gaza Strip risky, is keeping thousands of expatriates away.
The closure last year trapped some visitors in Gaza for weeks.
Under peace deals that launched Palestinian self-rule in parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, Israel maintains overall control over international crossing points.
Palestinians say many visiters languish for days at crossing points while waiting for Israeli permission to enter. Leaving the Gaza Strip is equally tedious.

Mohammed Hussein, in charge of the Palestinian passports department which coordinates family visits with Israel, says only a fraction of the Palestinians returning home annually have arrived so far this year.
Hussein said Israel granted just 16,000 entry permits last year compared with 35,000 in 1995. So far this year, Israel has issued just 2,500 permits.
"The number of applications for summer visits is far less than those filed last year," Hussein said.
Israel confirmed it was scrutinising entry requests more closely to ensure Palestinians returning for summer visits would not end up staying in Palestinian-ruled areas.

"We already have 35,000 people who came in the last few years and stayed in the Palestinian Authority (areas)," said Shlomo Dror, a spokesman for a senior Israeli defence official who holds the title of "coordinator of activities" in the West Bank and Gaza.
"What we are doing now is not to stop permits, but to check more carefully if people are coming to visit or to stay," he said.
COLLECTIVE PUNISHMENT
Palestinians argue that Israeli restrictions are a violation of peace accords which require Israel to afford Palestinians free travel in and out of the self-rule areas.
They maintain that Israeli measures are part of a policy of collective punishment against Palestinians.
"This is collective punishment intended to choke up the Palestinian economically, socially and politically," said Freij al-Khairi, deputy minister of civil affairs in the Palestinian Authority.
Palestinians say the Israeli restrictions includes barring children born in specific countries from accompanying their parents, thus effectively barring the entire family from the summer trips.
All of Abdel-Jawad's five children were born in the Gulf State of Qatar, a new addition to the blacklist which includes Syria, Lebanon, Libya, Iraq and Algeria.
Dalal said she had not seen her brother since he left Gaza some 30 years ago and was looking forward to seeing him this year.
"I wonder now if I will ever see him before I die," said the woman as she left the Palestinian passports department office.
